content.text: ASP.NET Core ships with a built-in

container. You register services once in Program.cs with a lifetime (Singleton, Scoped or Transient), ask for them in constructors, and the framework builds and disposes the objects for you. The classic production bug is a Singleton holding on to a Scoped service.
Open any ASP.NET Core project and you will see the same pattern: classes never call

on the services they depend on. Instead they list those dependencies as constructor parameters and something else hands them over. That something is the DI container, and understanding it is one of the first real steps from writing code that works to writing code that is easy to test and change.

. It is now welded to SMTP: you cannot swap in a different provider, and every unit test that touches orders tries to send a real email. Dependency Injection flips this around. The service declares what it needs, usually as an interface, and the caller decides which implementation to provide.

items.text: Swap implementations without touching the consumer (SMTP today, a cloud email API tomorrow).
Unit tests pass in fakes or mocks instead of real infrastructure.
Object lifetimes and disposal are managed in one place instead of all over the codebase.

content.text: An interface describes what the service does, not how.
A class implements the interface and asks for its own dependencies in its constructor.
In Program.cs, map the interface to the implementation on builder.Services.
Controllers, minimal API handlers and other services receive it as a parameter.

Every registration has a lifetime that decides how often the container creates a new instance. Picking the right one matters more than any other DI decision.

content.text: as Scoped by default, so each request gets its own change tracker. Services that use it should normally be Scoped too.

A Singleton that receives a Scoped service keeps that one instance alive for the whole application. With a DbContext this means one change tracker shared by every request and every thread, which leads to stale data, memory growth and threading exceptions. items.text: Depend on interfaces and ask for them in constructors.
Register once in Program.cs with the right lifetime; DbContext-based services are Scoped.
Never let a longer-lived service capture a shorter-lived one; use IServiceScopeFactory when you must.
Don't build the provider yourself and avoid the service locator in business code.
